rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible while mapping the overall elution window. This should reveal whether peaks are compressed early or late and provide a strong basis for narrowing the phi window and adjusting slope in the next runs.

All compounds eluted cleanly and the elution window sits well inside the gradient, so trim the gradient to roughly bracket the observed phi_e range and keep all peaks in-gradient. This should spend more of the run on the critical cluster around rows 5–7 while likely reducing total time further.

The narrow-window gradient improved resolution but cost too much time, so now test slope sensitivity directly from the successful broad window by halving tG. This will show whether the critical mid-cluster is strongly slope-dependent and may improve CRF by shortening the run while checking if minR stays acceptable.

The 10 min gradient is very fast but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min gave comfortable resolution; an intermediate slope should recover enough separation with only a modest time penalty. This directly brackets the slope optimum near the current best method.

The limiting pair improves strongly as the gradient is shallowed, and 14 min is close but still below baseline target, so a small increase to 16 min should lift the 6/7 separation further with only a small time increase. This is the most direct refinement around the current optimum.

The 6/7 pair is only weakly separated near the optimum slope, suggesting temperature may shift selectivity enough to improve it without sacrificing the zero time penalty of the 14 min method. A 5 °C decrease is a modest selectivity probe around the current best conditions.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing a different pair, so test the opposite direction at the current optimal slope. A 5 °C increase may improve the crowded mid-cluster separation while keeping run time essentially unchanged.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so stay at 40 °C and refine slope on the fast side of the optimum. Testing 12 min will map the CRF peak more precisely between the 10 and 14 min results and confirm whether 14 min is truly best.

The critical cluster elutes around phi_e roughly 0.28–0.37 and the last peak by about 0.58, so slightly lowering phi1 while keeping the proven 14 min slope may redistribute gradient space toward the crowded middle without pushing anything into the hold. This tests whether a modestly narrower high-end window can improve selectivity at essentially the same run time.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the limiting pair while keeping zero time penalty, so continue in the same direction with a slightly narrower window. The last peak still elutes comfortably in-gradient, making 0.85 a safe and informative next refinement.

The 0.90 window improved selectivity, but 14 min may now be slightly shallower than needed; shortening to 12 min could keep acceptable resolution while preserving the zero time penalty. This tests whether the better phi window supports a faster method with even higher CRF.

At phi1 = 0.90, 12 min is too steep and 14 min is close to optimal, so test 16 min to see whether the improved window can reach full resolution with only a minimal time penalty. This directly checks whether the current best can be nudged upward by a small gain in the limiting 6/7 pair.

Slope optimization appears nearly exhausted, so probe a larger temperature shift at the best phi window to see if selectivity for the limiting 6/7 pair changes nonlinearly. A 10 °C decrease is worth testing because 35 °C changed pair behavior substantially, indicating temperature-sensitive ordering in the crowded cluster.

The first peak is still quite early under the best conditions, so a small increase in phi0 may compress the uncritical early region and reallocate gradient space toward the crowded middle without greatly affecting the last peak. This is a focused test of window placement around the current best method.

Raising phi0 improved CRF, and lowering phi1 previously helped the critical pair, so combine both successful adjustments. This should further center gradient effort on the crowded middle while keeping the last peak safely inside the gradient.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so use the remaining budget to map robustness around the optimum. A small increase in phi0 tests whether the method sits on a broad plateau or whether 0.10 is a sharp optimum for the crowded central pair.

CRF remains at the maximum after raising phi0 to 0.15, so continue stepping phi0 upward to define the upper edge of the optimal plateau. This checks how far the start composition can be increased before early elution or loss of selectivity begins to hurt the score.

The optimum is clearly on a broad plateau near phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, so now test whether phi1 can be lowered one more step without sacrificing the limiting pair. This defines the lower edge of the plateau and checks if still tighter focusing of the useful gradient window preserves the maximum score.

Since both phi0 = 0.10 and phi1 = 0.80/0.85 look favorable, test the combined lower-window edge to complete mapping of the maximum-CRF region. This helps determine whether the optimum plateau extends across both successful settings or whether one boundary is sharper.

The maximum-score plateau includes phi0 = 0.15 with phi1 = 0.85, so test the adjacent higher phi1 boundary at the same phi0 to complete the local map around the optimum. This will clarify whether the plateau extends upward in phi1 or if 0.85 is the best-centered upper composition.

Now that the phi window giving maximum CRF is established, test whether that optimized window can tolerate a shorter gradient without losing too much of the critical 6/7 resolution. This probes the fast edge of the optimum basin around the best method.

Since phi0 = 0.15 also gave the maximum score at 14 min, test the faster 12 min gradient there to compare robustness of the two top methods on the steep side. This helps identify which maximum-CRF setting has the broader operating window.

We have mapped the steep side of the optimum; now test the shallow side for the best window to confirm the width of the maximum-CRF plateau in tG. This will show whether the 0.10/0.85 method remains fully resolved at 16 min or begins to incur only a small time penalty.

Complete the shallow-side comparison for the other maximum-CRF method to confirm that both top settings behave similarly as tG increases. This finishes mapping robustness around the optimum without repeating any condition.

For the final run, test the one remaining neighboring condition around the top plateau: phi0 = 0.10, phi1 = 0.90 at the shallow side. This completes the local response map around the two maximum-CRF methods and checks whether a slightly higher phi1 better balances resolution and time at 16 min.
